title: Incident tool responses include Diagnoses without the diagnoses:read scope
description: A valid MCP Credential can be issued with incidents:read while omitting diagnoses:read. Both MCP scope layers deny that Credential's direct get_diagnosis call, yet list_incidents and get_incident return the complete stored incident object, including Diagnosis rootCause, evidence excerpts, confidence and references. The affected data belongs to the Credential's own Project; the crossed boundary is the delegated MCP capability for reading Diagnoses. The source trace retains Project isolation but contains no scope-aware removal of the embedded Diagnosis. This is a source-only candidate, conditional on the real HTTP Project-context handoff reaching the backend; no disclosure was locally observed.
claimed_root_cause: Authorization is applied to primitive names while the incident tools reuse the full RecordedHaunting response shape. That shape includes the very Diagnosis object protected by the separate get_diagnosis permission. Generic string redaction preserves the object and its nonsecret private content, so it does not enforce the missing capability at the response projection.

title: Concurrent Work attempts can reuse a stale Project PR-limit decision
description: An OAuth client holding tokens:manage and fix:trigger may start fixes for two distinct eligible Work items in its granted Project. With maxOpenPrsPerHour set to one and no recent publication, both attempts can read zero before either saves an intent. The source evaluates that counter before routing and patch preparation, then admits each publication using only its own Work/attempt/lease checks. The hypothesized result is two draft-publication admissions under the owner's one-per-hour policy. Source review establishes the separate check and use paths; the concurrent result has not been observed.
claimed_root_cause: The Project-wide policy count is read and evaluated outside the publication transaction. Claimed/running attempts do not consume publicationCount, and beginPublication neither rechecks the configured maximum nor atomically reserves a Project-wide slot. Serializable transactions, command locks and version fences protect individual commands and Work records after the stale decision, so they do not bind publication to the shared limit that authorized it.

trace.description: An authenticated management client with fix:trigger submits separate Fix now commands for two Work IDs; caller() supplies the principal's Project and actor. The same downstream policy path also handles automatic triage.
The daemon verifies the caller Project, checks replay and eligibility, claims the selected Work item and invokes runFix. Distinct Work items and command IDs do not share a Work fence.
Each live attempt resolves its own context before evaluating policy. No Project-wide publication slot is acquired at this point.
The daemon obtains shared policy facts from the API's Project-qualified internal context endpoint.
After the Project grant and Diagnosis checks, resolve requests publicationCount and returns it as counters.openPrsLastHour. This read does not reserve capacity for the attempt.
Only attempts in the Project with non-null publication and recent updatedAt count. Both claimed/running attempts can therefore observe the same zero while neither has reached beginPublication.
The daemon computes one open_pr policy decision from those facts and, after audit acknowledgment, continues on allow through routing and patch preparation without refreshing the PR counter.
The intended control denies an open_pr action when openPrsLastHour is at least maxOpenPrsPerHour. Two earlier zero snapshots both pass a configured maximum of one.
The acknowledged pre-effect audit is followed by runtime.beginPublication. Neither operation refreshes the earlier shared-cap decision.

The publication change runs in a serializable transaction after locking the Project/command pair. Different command IDs have different locks, and the transaction does not include the prior policy-counter read.

The durable boundary checks only this Work snapshot, active attempt, owning command, live lease and absence of prior publication; it then saves the publishing intent and audit. It never checks or reserves maxOpenPrsPerHour across other Work items.

Each admitted attempt reaches prepared.publish after its own saved intent. A bounded local fixture should stop at two mock draft-publisher invocations or two durable publication intents under the configured maximum of one.

The strongest durable publication admission checks ownership, versions, live lease and saved intent, but not shared Project capacity.

The production drain wrapper starts each command promise and tracks it in a pending set; it does not serialize commands. main wires this wrapper to createCommandHandler.
The actual publication sink runs after individual admission, with no additional Project PR-limit check on this path.

title: Permanent Haunting-write failures retain expanding observation histories
description: A plugin Credential holder can send small valid detection Events with unique 180-character IDs. The public DTO and Event schema accept those IDs, but createObservations appends :detected:<rule> and sends that longer value to an internal DTO capped at 180 characters. Each write is therefore permanently refused after the accepted WatcherOutcome has entered the daemon's pending map. The consumer's five-delivery limit eventually stops retrying the broker record without notifying or evicting the cached outcome. With timestamps spaced by the watcher dedupe interval, later failed Events for the same bound service retain successive cloned histories containing one, two, three and more detections. This yields source-visible quadratic retained history across a linear number of small Events in the daemon shared by other granted Projects. No heap measurement, crash or service outage has been observed.
claimed_root_cause: The in-memory pending outcome cache has success-only cleanup and no terminal-failure, size or expiry policy. Public Event-ID validation is incompatible with derived internal idempotency-key limits, supplying a deterministic permanent-error trigger. createGrouper returns a deep clone of each cumulative group, so each abandoned pending outcome retains its own history rather than only one bounded reference.

trace.description: A Credential holder can choose a nonempty 180-character low-entropy alphabetic ID. The small envelope fits the API size limit and can use its bound service.
Preparation and publication retain the caller's ID after Project/service authorization. An unassigned Event audit key with this ID still fits the core 200-character audit-key contract.
The watcher is mutated and its accepted outcomes are saved in pending before any durable Haunting write completes.
Each accepted detection extends signalIds and detections, then returns a structured clone of the entire cumulative group. Ten-minute-spaced caller timestamps permit successive accepted detections.
The daemon derives eventId by adding :detected: and the rule name to the already 180-character Event ID.
The internal record route rejects this derived value through MaxLength(180), which the global validation pipe reports as an unprocessable request.
Failed observation processing requests redelivery; the declared consumer caps deliveries at five but has no terminal-outcome callback to the observation cache.
The rejected reduction bypasses pending.delete at line 206. Cached cloned histories remain reachable for the lifetime of the observation runtime after broker retry exhaustion.

evidence.description: The pending Map has no declared size, expiry, cancellation or terminal-delivery eviction policy. Its only deletion is after successful processing.
The shared ID schema imposes only nonemptiness, so envelope preparation does not reject the public 180-character input.
Global DTO validation applies the internal maximum and uses HTTP 422 for validation failures.
The private API client throws for the 422 response, propagating failure out of observation processing before cleanup.
Five broker deliveries and bounded broker retention do not remove objects retained in the separate observation closure.
The default 65536-byte Event cap and 60-per-minute throttle bound individual input and arrival rate, but not lifetime cached outcomes. The proposed inputs are under one KiB each.
One observation runtime is passed to the shared granted-Project consumer, so retained state occupies the daemon used by other Projects.

blockers: No bounded observation of retained pending entries, cloned-history growth or post-max-delivery cleanup was performed because complete memory and cumulative disk sandbox controls are unavailable.
Actual process-level resource impact and recovery have not been measured; the source trace does not establish a crash, outage or a deployed supervisor's behavior.

validation_plan.local: In a parent-approved sandbox, run createObservations with a Project-correct fake API that enforces the real RecordHauntingDto limit, a mocked gateway and no external Work action. Also verify one unrelated dummy Project can still process a normal record.

title: A co-tenant Event can prevent release of another Project's closed Haunting group
description: When one daemon serves two granted Projects using the same service name, a Credential holder in Project B can submit a valid warning Event for that service while B has no active Haunting. The active lookup for B deletes the service-only cache entry belonging to Project A, but its attempted release is restricted to B and leaves A's watcher group intact. If A's durable Haunting is closed before its next eligible detection, that detection reuses the unreleased group. The daemon loads the closed record, preserves its closed state and appends the new detection to it, rather than opening the new active Haunting expected by the existing single-Project close/reopen behavior. The minimum claimed boundary result is a new Project A detection being recorded on a closed Haunting because of Project B's Event.
claimed_root_cause: createObservations stores active IDs under service alone, although createGrouper stores groups under [projectId,service]. Cache deletion, replacement and release therefore refer to different namespaces. Durable Project checks protect row ownership but do not repair the stale group, and the merge path preserves the prior closed incident state.

trace.description: A Project B Credential can publish to its own bound service using a service name also present in Project A. A warning http.request Event can exercise the active lookup without creating a B detection.
A shared daemon legitimately accepts both granted Projects and serially invokes its one observation runtime.
Project B finds A's ID in byService, calls release(B,A-id), and deletes the service entry when B's active lookup returns null.
The Project equality check correctly refuses to delete A's group when release is called with B, so A's stale group remains while its cache entry is lost.
After A's durable Haunting closes, its next eligible detection finds the old [A,service] group and retains the old incident ID instead of creating a new group.
The get-by-ID call returns A's closed record. Spreading prior.incident after change.incident preserves the closed state while adding the new detection and updatedAt.
The Project, service, opening time and monotonic-update checks allow this update to the existing closed row; no new active Haunting is created for the detection.

Open groups are keyed by [detection.projectId,detection.service], so the watcher and bridge cache disagree about identity.
The authoritative active lookup excludes resolved and dismissed rows. Thus A's later null response is legitimate, but the missing service cache ID prevents release.
mergeRecorded accepts the next incident state, and hauntingData writes it directly to the row; there is no closed-to-new-detection lifecycle rejection.
The source checks returned active service, state and detection Project, but those checks do not scope byService itself.

Mock the gateway and Work port so the fixture performs no external or paid action.

title: Collector evidence selection drops Project authorization
description: A caller holding an MCP Credential for one granted Project can select any service name for tail_logs and any daemon-allowlisted metric job. The API supplies the authenticated Project and the daemon validates grant membership, but the final collector reads no longer receive that Project. Service inventory also includes all configured collectors. In a deployment where a shared daemon observes evidence reserved for another Project or Organization, the source path would return that evidence using the daemon's Docker, Kubernetes or Prometheus authority. Redaction can remove recognized sensitive strings while leaving private operational log text and numeric metrics visible. This requires a valid narrow-scope MCP Credential, a reachable real Project context, and a collector resource outside that Project's authorized scope; no such disclosure was executed or observed during this source-only review. The Event-driven diagnosis path reaches the same host-wide log reader: observations supplies an Event Project, but the production main callback drops it before ReadRuntime.logs. Ordinary private log text can therefore enter the wrong Project's model context under the same ownership conditions, independently of an MCP HTTP context handoff. No provider request or persisted diagnosis was observed.
claimed_root_cause: ReadRuntime treats collector evidence as host-wide after checking only whether the caller's Project appears in the daemon grant. Its logs and metric methods have no projectId parameter, inventory is not filtered by Project, CollectorReads has no Project ownership contract, and the configured metric allowlist is global. The service uniqueness check and namespace/job allowlists constrain selection but do not bind the selected resource to the authenticated Project.

title: Fix repository selection is not bound to the Work Project
description: A tenant able to publish evidence and initiate an eligible Fix in its own granted Project can name a service mapped by the instance policy to a repository outside that tenant's authority. contextClient checks the tenant's durable diagnosis and Deployment, but chooses the repository solely by service name. If the attacker registers a known commit from that repository as a Deployment in its own Project and the normal Fix policy allows the attempt, the daemon uses its operator GitHub App identity to fetch that repository for the attacker's Fix task. The affected resource is the other principal's repository/source context; the attacker need not possess a GitHub credential or membership in its owning Project. This candidate stops at the unauthorized repository-read/context-selection boundary and does not claim a verified patch, draft PR, merge or code execution. Independent review of the same trace from the patch-execution boundary confirms that repository selection uses only snapshot.item.service, that RepoPolicy has no Project selector, and that the final publication check repeats service membership only; a caller-supplied Deployment SHA in its own Project supplies a syntactically valid commit point.
claimed_root_cause: Project scope is preserved for Work, diagnosis, detections and Deployment records but is dropped at repository selection. The shared policy's repository records and service-based rules contain no Project grant, and neither contextClient nor prepareSource checks a caller-Project-to-repository authorization before using the instance GitHub identity.

trace.description: With its own Deployment-write authority, the tenant registers a supplied 40-hex SHA in its own Project. The service checks Organization and Project access, then appends the supplied SHA without repository ownership/provenance binding. This is a required prerequisite, not a Deployment-authentication bypass.

The plugin producer supplies service, its own projectId and the registered Deployment. Scope, Project equality, optional Credential service equality and same-Project Deployment lookup are enforced; the service is not resolved to a Project-owned repository.
The Event's diagnosed incident is saved in its Project, converted to a Work item and passed to onWork with that Project. A later eligible Fix remains a command on the attacker's own Work item.
The command checks the daemon Project grant, reads that Project's Work item, checks Fix eligibility and claims an attempt. The autoFix triage sibling reaches the same runFix path.
The repository filter compares only repo.services with snapshot.item.service. The unique match is selected before the subsequent caller-Project-bound context checks.

Strong diagnosis, service, confidence, category, detection-Project, signal and Deployment-SHA consistency checks bind the durable context, but the returned repo is never checked against caller.projectId.
The open_pr decision and its audit must permit the attempt. Its category/service/signal/counter gates cannot supply the missing Project-to-repository grant.
After audit-scope, Deployment-SHA, base-audit and configured-verification checks, the daemon passes input.context.repo, its GitHub client and the Project's Deployment SHA to prepareSource.
The claimed attempt resolves context with the authenticated caller and its Project-scoped Work snapshot.
Publication admission persists the chosen repo/branch/base under the caller's Project before invoking the prepared publication; it does not add a repository ownership check.
The last repository allowlist gate checks incident.service against repo.services and the patch path rules, with no Project selector.

client.getCommitTree(repo.repo, baseSha), followed by tree/blob reads, uses the instance GitHub identity without caller Project information. This is the minimum resource-authority boundary requiring validation.

evidence.description: One daemon grant supplies a Project set alongside a single instance policy and Agent list, rather than a policy/repository mapping for each Project.
Repository entries contain repo, services, base branch and patch constraints, but no Project owner/grant. Rule matching also lacks a Project selector.
Repository selection is the unique service-name match; caller.projectId is used only in later durable API reads and detection checks.
Deployment creation requires the tenant's legitimate org:ci or project:write authority. The candidate does not assume another Project's Deployment can be borrowed.
Deployment input validates the SHA format and metadata, while DeploysService.create checks the caller's own Project and stores the supplied SHA without repository verification.
Policy matching uses action, category, service and signals; confidence, counters and spend gates remain effective, but do not authorize the selected repository for a Project.

The last controls before source retrieval require a configured verification entry and audited base SHA. They do not inspect repository ownership, and the downstream source API accepts no caller Project.
One command runtime receives all boot.projectIds and one shared boot.policy/contextClient.
A delegated Credential binds the caller's Project and stores the requested service value; it does not reserve that service name across Projects.
Event guards enforce the credential's own Project/service and an own-Project Deployment lookup. They do not establish ownership of a GitHub repository named by a matching global service policy.
Deployment creation correctly checks own-Organization/Project authority, then stores the caller-supplied SHA without associating it with a repository. The DTO checks a 40-hex form.
The final publication target check is service membership only; the GitHub installation is selected later from the resulting repository string.

The owner must establish that a single daemon is granted mutually untrusted Projects and that a service-mapped repository is intended to be restricted to one of them. A deployment that deliberately shares repository authority across all granted Projects would not establish the claimed cross-principal violation.

title: Combined Compose service identity can carry platform authority into the demo image
description: The documented support-plus-demo composition reuses services.api for the platform API and lower-trust watched example. The demo supplies the haunted image and example build context, while normal Compose merging can retain the platform's internal/JWT/root-bootstrap environment fields and core network membership. An actor with write authority confined to examples/** can control the demo build/runtime inputs without editing platform configuration. The candidate requires an owner to enable the inherited api profile with nonempty platform credentials and a runnable demo image; it does not assert that the unchanged current combination leaks secrets. The source currently retains a platform Dockerfile path and src/main.ts command absent from the example, and no render or execution result was obtained.
claimed_root_cause: deploy/compose/graveshift.compose.yml and deploy/compose/demo.compose.yml assign different trust roles to the same Compose service key. The later demo definition overrides image/build context but does not clear inherited platform environment, networks, profile, command or build.dockerfile fields. Thus a runnable examples-controlled variant may receive the authority of the platform service instead of remaining a separate watched workload.

The candidate also applies to any equivalently scoped example contributor.

The example image copies its src tree and normally runs the demo API. An examples-only writer controls code packaged into that lower-trust image and can supply an examples-local Dockerfile/entrypoint matching fields retained by the combined service; no platform-source edit is needed for those files.

Support services.api is opt-in through profile api, uses the platform Dockerfile/command, includes API/daemon internal tokens, the OAuth JWT secret and optional root-bootstrap credentials, and joins core. Empty defaults and the profile gate are material prerequisites, not an observed grant.

The documented combined launch selects graveshift.compose.yml first and demo.compose.yml second, causing same-named service definitions to be merged. The API-profile variant additionally requires the owner to enable that declared profile.

The claimed minimum boundary result is a runnable lower-trust image receiving a dummy platform-secret marker; retained core membership is a second configuration effect to inspect, without assuming a successful management operation.

title: Publication recovery can accept a same-parent head with unverified content
description: A repository actor able to rewrite a generated bot branch can replace its head with a different tree whose sole parent is the admitted Deployment SHA. If the draft is still open and the attempt needs reconciliation, recovery checks the current PR head against the current ref and original parent, then records that draft as the completed Fix. It never compares the remote tree to the verified patch. The branch name includes verified hashes, but a writer can retain that name while changing its content. The affected boundary is Graveshift's verification/result authority: the candidate claims acceptance of an unverified draft head, not GitHub write privilege gain for a writer, automatic merge, or release execution. Branch permissions and a bounded acceptance result remain unvalidated.
claimed_root_cause: The immutable object identity is lost when planPublication reduces the receipt to repo/branch/baseSha and PublicationIntent persists only those fields. getExistingDraft binds the current head/ref to the base parent but does not bind its tree or head digest to the original verified result. Both existing-draft reuse and uncertain-effect reconciliation trust this weaker identity.

trace.description: An authenticated replay of an uncertain publication parses the persisted intent containing repo, branch and baseSha, with no expected result tree or head. The lower-trust input is the current remote branch/PR state a repository writer can have replaced.
Recovery forwards only the recorded repository, mutable branch name and base SHA to the GitHub client and checks the returned repository/branch.
The client requires a unique open draft with the exact head ref in the same repository, preventing fork/ref confusion but not modification of the named branch.

It reads the remote commit's SHA and parents plus the current ref. The schema omits tree identity; acceptance requires only matching current head/ref and one parent equal to the recorded base. A different tree with that parent satisfies these checks.
The returned head reference is recorded under the original attempt and base. API recordPublication checks intent repository/branch/base and known-reference equality, not the verified tree.

The Work attempt is finished as completed with ok:true and the recovered head, without rerunning source verification. The minimal result to validate is recording a harmless substituted tree as the verified Fix.

evidence.description: planPublication validates the local receipt but returns only repository, deterministic branch and original base SHA.
Snapshot and patch hashes influence the branch name; they are not independently recovered from remote content.
The durable PublicationIntent schema has no expected head, expected tree or verified content digest.
The strongest remote check verifies PR head/ref consistency and a single parent equal to baseSha, with no content-identity comparison.
The normal publication path also returns a recovered existing draft immediately, without creating the verified content again or checking its remote tree.
The durable consumer checks repository/branch/base equality and fences state, but accepts the first recovered head because the intent has no expected content identity.
Source tests exercise wrong base, merge/root commits, moved refs and mismatched heads; no same-parent/different-tree binding is represented. These tests were not executed.

blockers: The assignment prohibits project execution, and the audit environment has no approved complete memory/cumulative-disk sandbox, so the same-parent/different-tree acceptance path has not been observed locally.

Actual GitHub rulesets, branch protections and the ability of a lower-trust repository actor to rewrite the bot branch are not visible in the reviewed source. A deployment that forbids such writes may prevent this attack condition.

A fixture must distinguish ordinary collaborator editing from a verification-authority failure by observing the exact substituted head being recorded as the original completed Fix; no broader release or merge consequence is established.

Persist a real-shaped uncertain intent for the originally verified tree, then return an open draft whose named branch and current head both point to the second tree. Exercise getExistingDraft and daemon replay reconciliation with fake durable state. Observe whether the second head becomes the completed result, and also check publishVerified's existing-draft shortcut. A regression must require a persisted expected tree/head identity and reject the second object before recording completion. Use dummy hashes, no live GitHub, and no retained artifacts until parent promotion is available.

title: macOS verifier cleanup targets one process group instead of all descendants
description: When a configured verification command executes repository-controlled code on macOS, that code can attempt to start a detached child in another process group. The source sandbox permits child creation, but the supervisor kills only the original command group. A descendant retaining inherited stdout can keep the close event and verification promise pending beyond the deadline; one using ignored stdio can instead remain alive after a successful return and during parent workspace inspection. This crosses the untrusted-check lifetime boundary into shared daemon work/process resources. The candidate is limited to retained work and potential concurrent writers; no host-file disclosure, actual service exhaustion or sandbox credential escape has been demonstrated.
claimed_root_cause: sandbox.execute treats process.kill(-child.pid) as complete teardown and resolves only from child.close. The macOS sandbox profile allows fork and same-sandbox child groups but supplies no descendant supervisor or process namespace. Changing session/group therefore falls outside the only kill target, while neither the timer nor verification independently terminates the pending operation or proves all writers are gone.

trace.description: A policy-accepted patch or repository file is executed by an operator-configured verification command. This condition requires a command that actually executes repository-controlled code; Git diff-only checks do not provide it.
The platform chooses sandbox-exec with macProfile. The policy permits process-fork and same-sandbox child operations, without Linux's PID namespace.
The trusted supervisor starts a detached command group with piped stdout. Repository-controlled code can attempt to create another detached group and retain the pipe or ignore stdio.
Cleanup and the timeout signal only -child.pid. They do not enumerate or own the detached descendant group, and the timer does not independently reject the promise.
Completion waits for close, which can remain pending while a separate descendant holds stdout. Conversely, ignored-stdio descendants need not prevent close and are not proven dead before returning.

While the verification promise remains pending, the attempt scope can continue its lease heartbeat; its finally block has not run. A closed-stdio survivor instead overlaps verifyPatch's post-command workspace inspection.

The daemon retains and drains pending Work promises, so a verification operation that outlives its deadline can also retain graceful drain. The minimal bounded observation is one dummy descendant or operation surviving a short deadline, not a stress test.

evidence.description: The sole termination target is the original negative child PID/process group.
The timer sets timedOut and calls stop but does not reject or resolve a still-open child result independently.
Only close resolves a running command; waiting on inherited stdout is therefore outside the timer's direct control.
The macOS policy permits process-fork. Unlike the Linux branch's --unshare-all path, it does not create a process namespace or bind all descendants to a supervisor-owned lifetime.

An existing source test intentionally spawns a detached child group from a sandboxed process and explicitly signals that group itself. It does not test supervisor cleanup after the parent exits or times out; the test was not run.
Host-side assertWorkspace follows a returned command, and finally removes the root at line 229 without a proof that every descendant has exited.
The HTTP handler bounds waiting with within(result), but the underlying command promise remains owned by drainCommands; this does not supply descendant cleanup.

blockers: The supported macOS sandbox-exec and runtime process/pipe lifecycle must be observed with a harmless detached-child fixture. Source declarations and unexecuted tests are insufficient to confirm OS behavior.

Target-controlled execution is prohibited for this assignment, and complete OS-enforced memory, process, CPU, per-file, cumulative-disk, filesystem and wall-clock controls for an audit fixture have not been established.

The deployed verifier must run on macOS with a command that executes repository-controlled code; actual configured commands and any outer descendant supervisor are operator-owned facts. The Linux PID-namespace path is not claimed vulnerable to this exact lifetime escape.

validation_plan.local: After the parent supplies a complete OS sandbox on a disposable macOS host, run one harmless fixture through runSandboxed with a short deadline. Have it spawn at most one detached child that self-terminates within a small fixed outer limit. In one case the child keeps stdout open; record whether the operation settles by its deadline. In a second case it ignores stdio and writes one dummy marker inside the fixture workspace after foreground completion; record whether it survived supervisor cleanup. Capture elapsed time and at most one PID/marker, then terminate and reap every fixture process. Do not fork repeatedly, allocate large memory, fill disk, inspect host processes, or access credentials. The regression must prove all descendants are gone before success, failure, timeout, post-command inspection and workspace removal.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should inspect the daemon OS, the verification argv for the affected repository, and whether an outer job/process supervisor tears down every descendant. This is a read-only configuration review and does not require running a check on the deployed daemon.

title: Password changes leave other pre-change Account bearers usable
description: A holder of a copied, still-valid Account bearer can continue using it after the legitimate Account holder changes the password, for the remainder of the one-hour token lifetime. For the bootstrap Account, a bearer issued while mustChangePassword is true also becomes owner-capable when somebody else completes the password change. The source has no session-specific state that distinguishes the current caller's bearer from another holder's bearer. The candidate requires prior possession of a valid token and stops at authority within that Account's own Organization; it does not establish a way to obtain a token or gain deployment-wide administration.
claimed_root_cause: Account JWTs contain no session identifier or password epoch. setPassword changes only passwordHash and mustChangePassword, while AccountAuthGuard verifies the static signing key and current Account/Membership state without checking an issuance epoch or revocation state. Clearing mustChangePassword therefore affects every unexpired token for that Account, including separately held first-login tokens. Preserving the current password-changing session may be intentional, but this representation cannot invalidate other sessions separately.

trace.description: An Account login before the password change issues the bearer later held by the attacker. The attacker must already possess this valid token.
The bearer contains Account sub/email and a 3600-second expiry, with no session identifier or password-version binding.
The legitimate holder uses a separate session to change the Account password; the service verifies the current password before writing the new hash.
Only passwordHash and mustChangePassword are updated. No bearer-revocation state is changed.

The old bearer still passes signature/audience verification before expiry. The stored Account exists, and its current mustChangePassword false value removes the first-login restriction for all such bearers.
The stale bearer supplies the same Account id, whose existing owner Membership and same-Organization Project satisfy the otherwise correct authorization checks.
A holder of the pre-change token can create a new Project-bound OAuth client under the Account's Organization without knowing the new password.

evidence.description: Account token issuance binds only sub/email, static issuer/audience/key and one-hour expiration.
Changing the password correctly requires the current password, but the successful path does not revoke or rotate pre-existing bearer state.
The password write changes only passwordHash and mustChangePassword.
The strongest current-state controls reload Account and Memberships; they do not compare token issue time/version with the password change. The first-login gate uses the Account's current boolean.
Account has no session version, password-change time or revocation relation that the guard could consult.
The existing test expects a pre-change token to work after the root password change. This was read as source, not executed, and does not cover invalidating a separately held token.

blockers: A bounded two-session lifecycle check was not executed because the assignment prohibits target-controlled execution without complete OS memory and cumulative disk controls. The required local observation of stale-token authorization is therefore unavailable.

validation_plan.local: After the parent establishes the complete sandbox, create a dummy owner Account, its Organization and one dummy Project. Issue two bearer sessions at distinct controlled clock instants. Use the second session and the current dummy password to change the password, then try exactly one protected OAuth-client creation with the first bearer before its original expiry. Repeat the transition with a dummy bootstrap Account: verify the first bearer is blocked while mustChangePassword is true, change the password through the second session, then try that first bearer once. Stop at the first dummy client record or rejection. Do not exchange the resulting client secret, contact external services or use real credentials.

title: Email-based member addition can select an attacker who registered the intended member's email first
description: An unauthenticated attacker can register a not-yet-registered person's email with an attacker-chosen password, without controlling that mailbox. If an Organization owner later adds the intended person by that email, the implementation immediately grants membership to the attacker's Account. The attacker can discover that Organization through profile and read its Project metadata or create Projects through the normal member routes. This requires the owner's independent add-member action; registration alone does not grant access to an existing Organization.
claimed_root_cause: register treats syntactic email validity as sufficient to reserve the global Account identity. addMember subsequently treats the same unverified email as the authority for selecting the person who receives a protected Membership. There is no mailbox-verification state or email-bound invitation acceptance between those two operations. The owner check is present and correctly scoped, but it authenticates the grantor without authenticating the intended recipient's email ownership.

trace.description: Public POST /api/register accepts the intended member's email and an attacker-chosen password without a bearer or mailbox challenge.
The email check establishes format and length; the request contains no proof of control of that email.
The email is stored with the attacker's password hash and mustChangePassword false. A previously unclaimed email is sufficient.
The attacker authenticates using the password chosen during registration and obtains a bearer for the preclaimed Account.
An existing Organization owner independently submits the intended person's email to the member-addition route.
The correctly scoped owner check passes, then the unverified email resolves directly to the attacker's Account and addMemberToOrg writes its member Membership.
The attacker's valid bearer resolves to the stored Account, and its newly granted Membership satisfies the Organization gate.
The attacker obtains orgId from its profile and now passes requireMembership for the owner's Organization.
The normal scoped query returns that Organization's Project records to the attacker-selected Account.

evidence.description: Account has a unique email and passwordHash but no email-ownership verification state; registration can reserve the identity before the intended person.
Registration performs uniqueness lookup and password hashing, then adds the Account without mailbox verification.
The strongest visible control is requireOwner(accountId, orgId); recipient selection nevertheless uses findAccountByEmail and immediately inserts membership.
The attacker's own profile lists its Organization ids, so no unknown orgId is required after the owner grants membership.
Project creation requires only Membership in the selected Organization, providing a bounded mutation consequence in addition to Project listing.

blockers: No dummy-principal HTTP or service fixture was executed. Target-controlled execution is prohibited because complete OS-enforced memory and cumulative disk controls are unavailable; source inspection alone does not satisfy the required observed-boundary-result gate.

validation_plan.local: After the parent establishes every required sandbox control, use only dummy Accounts, a dummy Organization and one dummy Project. Register an attacker-controlled password under intended-member@identity.test without mailbox proof and log in. Have a separate legitimate dummy owner add that email. With the attacker's bearer, read its own profile and request the dummy Organization's Project list. Stop at the first dummy Project returned or Membership exposed. Include a negative case requiring recipient email proof before that Membership becomes usable; do not contact mail systems or real people.

title: Public identity routes bypass the configured throttle before password work
description: Small valid unauthenticated registration requests trigger Argon2id hashing and Account insertion, while login requests naming an existing Account trigger password verification even when the password is wrong. AccountController does not use the configured ThrottlerGuard. If upstream admission and Bun's effective worker/queue controls do not protect the shared API budget, anonymous password work could reduce availability for other Organizations. The source establishes the admission gap and input-to-work path, not a measured service outage or unbounded native worker count.
claimed_root_cause: ThrottlerModule is configured without a global guard, and the public identity controller omits the per-route guard that OAuth token exchange explicitly installs. The identity service submits password work without a source-visible per-IP/global work budget or submission bound. Per-field and parser size limits do not stop repeated small requests. Runtime worker limits and deployed upstream controls may constrain the impact and are not assumed absent.

trace.description: Public registration and the adjacent auth/login handler accept requests without an authentication or throttle guard.
A configured throttler does not cover these routes automatically: AppModule registers no APP_GUARD and the identity module provides no alternative admission guard.
A short syntactically valid email and 12-to-256-character password pass validation; a large request body is unnecessary.
An unused email passes the uniqueness lookup and reaches password hashing without a submission budget. Repeated unique emails avoid the duplicate-account early exit.

Registration submits Argon2id work to Bun.password.hash; the independent existing-email login variant submits Bun.password.verify at line 92. These costs occur in the shared API process before successful authentication.

evidence.description: Neither public identity handler has ThrottlerGuard; protected handlers explicitly declare their AccountAuthGuard.
The application configures a rate limit but does not install it globally.
The sibling public OAuth token route explicitly installs ThrottlerGuard, showing the guard-based enforcement used elsewhere.
An accepted unused email causes Argon2id hashing followed by durable Account creation.
A known email causes password verification even when the attempt will return UnauthorizedException; unknown emails skip this cost.
Input length limits are effective per request but do not bound aggregate submissions or work already admitted.
The optional support API publishes on loopback. This is a visible reachability constraint; public routing and any upstream work limits cannot be inferred from this scaffold.

blockers: No bounded admission fixture or native password-cost observation was run because target execution is prohibited without complete OS memory and cumulative disk controls.

The effective upstream rate/concurrency limits, reachable identity-route topology, Bun password-worker queue/concurrency bounds and shared API resource budget are not established. Without them, a meaningful cross-Organization availability effect cannot be asserted.

validation_plan.local: Once a complete sandbox is available, configure a dummy identity application with a rate limit of one and replace password hashing/verification with bounded deferred mocks. Submit only two small requests per registration/login variant and record whether the second reaches the password-work mock or is rejected before admission. Inspect worker/queue configuration rather than stressing real Argon2. Use a separately bounded dummy request to determine which resources are shared, then stop; do not perform saturation testing.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should inspect the actual API ingress or local caller boundary, per-IP and aggregate admission policy, Bun password-work queue limits, and API CPU/memory isolation. Establish whether those controls cap anonymous admitted work below the shared resource budget and how pending work is cleared. This is a configuration and capacity review, not a request to send traffic to a deployed service.

title: Kiro shell hook guard guesses the event shape and fails open outside a finite command denylist
description: The tracked `block-dangerous-shell` hook runs `node scripts/kiro/guard-shell.mjs` on every shell tool call. The script does not bind to any in-repo Kiro event schema: it reads stdin, heuristically JSON-parses it, probes eight guessed field locations for a command, and on a read error, an unrecognized shape, or an empty string returns '' and exits 0, which the repository's own documentation says allows the tool. Even when a command string is extracted, the decision is a single regex over the literal text, so semantically destructive variants (for example `rm -rf /;true`, `git push origin +main`, `git -c foo=bar push origin main`, `kubectl -n ns delete pod`) are not blocked. The sibling `secret-scan-on-save` hook repeats the shape-guessing pattern and also fails open, reading an arbitrary path from event JSON. The only statements of Kiro's exit-code contract and hook principal are repository-authored; no vendor schema, payload fixture, or runtime source is present, so exploitability depends on facts outside the repository.
claimed_root_cause: The guard treats unverified, event-supplied structure as trusted control input: `extractCommand` enumerates guessed JSON paths and falls back to allow (exit 0) whenever the actual event shape differs, and enforcement is a literal regex that misses semantically equivalent destructive commands. The event-shape, hook-enforcement, and hook-principal facts needed to decide whether a lower-trust tool/save event can reach that fail-open path are external to the repository and cannot be assumed.

trace.scope: PreToolUse hook definition for the shell tool
trace.description: The hook fires on PreToolUse with matcher `shell` and runs the fixed command string `node scripts/kiro/guard-shell.mjs`; no event data is interpolated into the command.
Any stdin read failure is swallowed and converted to an empty string, removing the guard's only input.
Eight guessed JSON locations are probed; an actual Kiro shape outside this list, or a parse result that is not a string/object, yields '' with no error.
The security decision is one literal regex over the extracted command; semantic equivalents of the listed destructive commands do not match.

trace.scope: PreToolUse verdict on the developer host
trace.description: On no match (including an empty extracted command) the script exits 0, which the repository states permits the shell tool to run.

evidence.description: Fixed `action.command` runs the guard script; the command string is not event-controlled.
The complete DANGEROUS denylist is a single finite regex over literal text.
readStdin catch returns '' on any read error.
extractCommand returns '' when no guessed field holds a string.
Exit 0 is reached for empty or unmatched commands.
Sibling save hook reads a path taken from guessed event fields with hook-process privileges.
The only exit-code/trigger statement is a repo-authored claim about Kiro CLI v3; no vendor source corroborates it.
Strongest source-visible control: restricted agents deny shell and all fs_write, and their allowed write paths exclude the hook config and scripts.

blockers: No Kiro CLI v3 PreToolUse/PostFileSave stdin event schema, payload fixture, or vendor runtime source exists in the repository, so it cannot be established whether the eight guessed command paths (or twelve guessed file paths) cover the real event.

Kiro's hook enforcement semantics are not source-visible: exit 2 blocking, exit 1 warning, and the behavior on launch failure, timeout, or non-2 exit are asserted only in repo-authored comments and KIRO_USAGE.md.

The principal, working directory, PATH/environment, and shell used to execute the hook `action.command` are not declared in tracked configuration; the relative script path presumes cwd is the repository root.

No complete OS-enforced memory, process, CPU, file, disk, and wall-clock sandbox is established, so no bounded local check of the guard with a representative event was run and no observed result can be reported.

Do not execute the embedded commands.
validation_plan.deployment: On a developer host, an owner records the actual PreToolUse shell payload with a benign echo hook, confirms the exit-2 blocking contract with a harmless command, and confirms the hook process's user, cwd, and environment; no destructive command is run.

title: Docker restart selection can cross Compose project boundaries
description: When a Blessing is intended to restart one Project's worker service, a caller holding that fresh signed request can potentially cause the actuator's Docker identity to restart unrelated worker containers in other Compose projects on the same daemon. The writer selects all running containers with the service label and invokes restart for every returned ID. The request can remain exactly as approved and correctly signed; the unresolved issue is which resources that service name resolves to. This requires an enabled act-mode configuration, shared-daemon co-tenancy, per-project approval intent and a proxy that exposes both projects. The checked-in configuration is propose, and the in-repo platform-to-actuator producer is deferred. No deployed exposure or runtime effect was observed.
claimed_root_cause: The trusted resource resolver in createDockerRestarter authorizes by com.docker.compose.service alone. ActionRequest has no signed Project or Compose-project scope, policy checks only the service name, and the backend neither adds a trusted com.docker.compose.project predicate nor verifies ownership of the returned container IDs before fan-out. A valid approval for one scoped service can therefore name a broader host-level resource set when projects share service names.

The executor strictly parses the action and verifies its HMAC; this prevents mutation but authenticates only the resource fields present in the schema.
Admission checks the approval identity, action/incident binding, time, policy and action count for the signed service name.
The explicit target allowlist compares ctx.service to rule service strings and cannot distinguish different Compose projects with the same service name.
A successful unique token/action claim commits before execution. This correctly prevents replay of the request but does not narrow its resolved container membership.
The backend receives only action.service; no Project or Compose-project identity is supplied.
The Docker list filter contains only com.docker.compose.service=<service>. The returned set is not checked against another ownership predicate.
The actuator sends POST /containers/<Id>/restart for every returned ID under the host proxy's Docker authority, potentially including the unrelated project's same-named service.

The signature covers the entire accepted action, approval and context, which prevents tampering but cannot bind a resource scope absent from that object.
The sole lookup predicate is the Compose service label; lines 38-46 restart every returned container.
The production launcher instantiates this backend from DOCKER_PROXY_URL without an additional Project or Compose-project binding.

The maintained actuator proxy mounts the host Docker socket and enables container access, POST and restarts. No project-specific filtering is expressed here; effective image and deployment behavior remain unverified.
The committed default mode is propose, so activation of the runtime sink requires an owner-reviewed act-mode configuration.
The platform-to-actuator producer is described as a future action hop rather than part of the current Fix path. Reachability from a real approval producer must be established separately.

blockers: No backend or Docker fixture was executed: complete OS-enforced memory and cumulative disk sandbox controls are unavailable, and this assignment prohibits project code, tests, builds, containers and external requests. No local effect or retained artifact exists.

The effective pinned proxy's resource filtering, shared-daemon co-tenancy, enabled act configuration and intended per-project scope of the approval producer were not observed. The manifest alone does not establish a deployed cross-project boundary.

Provide two dummy container records representing distinct Compose projects with the same worker service. Inspect an available pinned Docker/proxy implementation or isolated dummy daemon to verify the service-label filter semantics. Keep external networking disabled and stop at the recorded wrong-target invocation.

Establish whether the proxy can enumerate and restart separate Compose projects, whether same-named services coexist, whether act mode is enabled, and whether each approval is intended to cover one Project. A dedicated daemon or effective resource filter would refute the deployed cross-project condition.

title: Runtime admission substitutes zero for authoritative policy usage
description: In a supported act-mode configuration, a submitter holding a still-valid signed Blessing issued before usage limits were reached can potentially execute a restart after recorded diagnosis-loop or Project daily-spend limits require denial. Runtime admission supplies zero for those quantities instead of obtaining current recorded usage, while the canonical policy gate applies both limits to runtime actions. Correct HMAC, an allowed human approver, target allowlisting, safe scale bounds and the local runtime action count remain required. The affected boundary is the admission owner's current policy decision under the actuator's Docker or Kubernetes authority. The shared helper is used by both the active local SQLite path and the optional API claim path. No runtime acceptance or backend effect was observed.
claimed_root_cause: claims.runtimeDecision reconstructs SharedPolicyContext with diagnosisLoops: 0 and llmSpentTodayUsd: 0 for every request. These are authoritative state facts, not known-zero properties of a runtime operation. ContextSchema cannot carry them, AdmissionRules has no usage reader, and neither SQLite admission nor API ActionRepo resolves the recorded Project/incident usage before calling this helper. PolicyContextService and AuditRepo already demonstrate the authoritative values and fail-closed handling elsewhere, but runtime admission bypasses that dependency.

trace.description: The request holder submits an unconsumed signed runtime action whose approval interval still includes the delivery time.
Strict parsing and HMAC verification authenticate the action, approval and available context. The signed context has no authoritative usage counters.
The active store obtains its clock and per-service action count and calls admissionDecision. It has no dependency that reads recorded diagnosis-loop or daily-spend usage.
The helper passes zero diagnosisLoops and zero llmSpentTodayUsd into the canonical policy engine, irrespective of the real recorded state.
This gate denies runtime actions when either actual usage quantity reaches its configured limit, but the substituted zeros pass positive limits when the other checks pass.

title: Event replay keys cross Project boundaries
description: A plugin Credential holder confined to one Project controls its Event IDs. If it knows or predicts an ID used by a different granted Project, it can submit an otherwise valid warning Event with that ID first. The shared consumer subsequently acknowledges the other Project's Event as already completed without dispatching its detection. A warning Event whose type does not produce detections can seed this state without a model call. Publisher msgID uses the same unscoped ID in the all-Project stream, creating a second place where the collision may suppress delivery. The claimed result is suppression of a target Project's observation; target-ID knowledge and a shared stream/consumer are explicit prerequisites.
claimed_root_cause: Project authority is present in the subject and body but omitted from replay identity: createNatsPublisher sends msgID=prepared.id and processQueued checks/marks a single shared Set using envelope.id. The API preserves producer-chosen IDs and does not establish global uniqueness. A 100000-entry size bound limits retained keys but does not isolate them.

trace.description: The producer supplies any nonempty string as its Event ID; the contract adds no Project namespace or globally unique server ID.
Scope, Project and service binding are enforced, then the original Event ID is preserved through preparation and publication.
Every Project uses prepared.id alone as the broker msgID, while the subject includes its Project.
The one stream spans all Project subjects and declares a 120-second duplicate window.
Both dummy Projects can legitimately pass the granted set; their distinct subjects and bodies pass exact reconstruction.
After the first Project's successful processing marks the ID at line 113, an Event with the same ID from the second Project is acknowledged and returned without calling process.

evidence.description: The completed-ID Set has one global string namespace and only an oldest-entry size eviction.
One deduplicator is created for the consumer serving every granted Project.
An accepted envelope type with no watcher outcomes still finishes observation processing, allowing the transport to mark its ID completed.
The watcher uses [projectId,id] for replay identity, demonstrating the stronger downstream namespace that the consumer bypasses.
Size, schema, exact subject equality and granted-Project controls are present; none changes the unscoped replay key after both valid Projects pass.

blockers: No bounded in-memory producer/consumer observation was performed: complete memory and cumulative disk sandbox controls are not established, and the assignment forbids target-code execution.
The publisher-side stream-wide msgID collision still needs a bounded observation against the pinned NATS version; no broker, deployed endpoint or external service was contacted.

validation_plan.local: In a parent-approved sandbox, feed a createEventsConsumer fake transport two small valid warning envelopes for dummy Projects 101 and 202 with ID shared-event, and record process calls and acknowledgements. Use a no-detection type for the first Event. Stop after checking whether the second Project is acknowledged without dispatch. Independently inspect publisher options for distinct Project IDs, then use a bounded isolated broker fixture to establish msgID behavior. A regression should allow one dispatch per [Project,Event ID] while still deduplicating a replay within the same Project.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner can inspect effective stream/consumer sharing and producer ID-generation rules to establish whether a co-tenant could know or predict a target ID. This requires configuration and producer-source inspection, without sending live test Events.

title: A permanently rejected workload name can block the shared Collector queue
description: An enabled Kubernetes Collector watches multiple configured namespaces through one ordered queue. A less-trusted workload owner who can choose a legal name containing a dummy model-key-shaped substring, such as demo-sk-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa, can produce a Warning Event that maps to an observation whose service fails privacy validation. The queue retries that deterministic failure forever, blocking later observations from other watched workloads. The Docker variant uses a producer-controlled com.docker.compose.service label containing a dummy email such as ops@example.invalid. The affected resource is the Collector's observation lane; no process crash or suppression beyond that Collector is claimed. Each variant requires delegated workload metadata authority and normally functioning Collector publication.
claimed_root_cause: createDeliveryQueue retries all entry.deliver and publisher errors indefinitely without distinguishing permanent validation failures, enforcing an attempt/deadline limit, or quarantining the head record. Both Collectors prepare workload-derived service metadata inside entry.deliver, where assertSafeMetadata can always reject it. The queue's 256-record bound and one-second manual stop deadline do not allow healthy records past that head during normal operation.

trace.description: A schema-valid Warning Event carries the workload's involvedObject.name into involvedName. The parser has no privacy-pattern restriction on workload names.
An included namespace's workload name becomes the qualified Grave service and mapped runtime Event details in one shared Collector queue.

entry.deliver constructs its envelope using the workload-derived service before sending it. A name such as demo-sk-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa retains a word boundary before the key-shaped substring even after qualification.
The helper passes Context.service into prepareEnvelope, preserving the workload-derived selector as routing metadata.
The model-key detector matches the dummy sk- substring and rejects the non-UUID service with EnvelopeError on every attempt.
The same permanent validation exception is caught and retried with capped backoff until the queue is externally stopped.
The worker never reaches acknowledge, pending.shift or notification for the poison head, so later unrelated workload records cannot publish through this Collector.

evidence.description: The explicit model-key regex accepts a sk- prefix followed by at least twenty allowed characters, including the dummy all-letter example.
Service and fingerprint are privacy-checked routing metadata rather than redacted payload fields.
A full queue aborts the push watch, but finally waits on queue.drain; this cannot bypass a permanently failing head or reconnect to healthy later records.

The Docker variant trusts the com.docker.compose.service attribute for service and constructs its envelope inside the same retrying delivery callback at lines 99-110. An email-shaped label deterministically fails the separate email metadata detector.
ready prevents more than 256 pending records but keeps Docker waiting behind the head. stop at line 123 provides manual bounded cancellation, not automatic quarantine.

The active daemon factory can enable Docker and Kubernetes Collectors, each sharing one queue across its collected workloads. The effective enabled deployment and delegated workload authority are not established by this source-only review.

blockers: No small poison-then-healthy Collector fixture was executed because complete memory and cumulative disk sandbox controls are unavailable.
The owner must establish actual delegated metadata authority and enabled Collector namespace/endpoint scope. Direct host-root control alone would not establish a lower-trust Docker principal.

Normal daemon reader/publisher authentication must be established from effective wiring. Compose does not launch the daemon, and the checked-in NATS read user's permissions alone do not authorize detection publication.

validation_plan.local: In a parent-approved sandbox, use the native Collector interface with a fixed clock, an in-memory publisher and exactly two native records. First emit a Kubernetes Warning/ImagePullBackOff Event for Pod demo-sk-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa-5d8f9c7b6d-x2k4q in an included dummy namespace, then a healthy-named Warning record in another included dummy namespace. Allow a fixed small number of injected backoff steps, then stop. Record whether the first record repeatedly fails preparation and the second never reaches the publisher. Repeat the independent Docker variant with com.docker.compose.service=ops@example.invalid followed by another container's record. A regression should quarantine or explicitly refuse permanent-invalid input and allow the second record to progress while retaining retry semantics for transient failures.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner can inspect manifests, delegated workload roles, enabled Collector settings and effective NATS permissions to establish that a lower-trust workload owner can choose these names/labels and shares a normally functional observation lane with another workload. Do not create workloads or send poison records in a deployed environment.

title: Allowed telemetry strings may cause superlinear synchronous redaction before truncation
description: A producer holding a service-bound plugin Credential can submit a valid Sentry event with a long alphabetic event.type below the one-MiB envelope limit. The mapper redacts that entire string before truncating its normalized type to 128 characters, and its payload projection can omit the original top-level type. The shared email detector has an unanchored greedy local-part expression that can repeatedly scan suffixes of a non-matching token. This creates a source-grounded candidate from one Project's telemetry capability to CPU work on the shared API process; the final Event can be small enough for the broker cap. Plugin payload and identity processing reach the same detector under the smaller plugin request cap. No timing, service interruption, or cross-Project delay was demonstrated, and no severity is assigned.
claimed_root_cause: The shared redactor applies an unanchored, potentially quadratic email regex synchronously to caller-controlled strings without a per-string work budget. Sentry eventType invokes it before the only type-length truncation. The strongest visible controls are the one-MiB Sentry raw/parser caps, the plugin default 65,536-byte and maximum 102,400-byte cap, client request throttling, four redaction passes, and a downstream 128-KiB stream message limit. They bound request count, total bytes, passes, or final publication size, but do not establish linear regex work or preempt a synchronous call. Whether the supported Bun engine optimizes this pattern enough to prevent meaningful shared impact is unresolved.

trace.description: A throttled caller with a valid plugin publish Credential submits an envelope; Project and service remain constrained by SentryKeyGuard.
The route accepts a raw envelope up to one MiB; it does not impose a separate maximum on the JSON event.type string.
The parser checks whole-envelope and event-item byte caps and parses an event JSON object without a per-field string-length bound.
The accepted event object is passed to mapSentryEvent before final envelope validation or broker publication.
The raw exception type or event.type is passed to redact in full at line 25; the 128-character slice occurs afterward at line 28. A long top-level event.type is not copied into the mapped payload.
The synchronous detector loop calls String.replace for the email expression on the API request's execution path; the maximum of four passes does not limit the work of one match attempt.

The unanchored [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+ local part followed by a required @ can rescan successive suffixes of a long non-matching alphabetic token. Engine behavior and meaningful shared CPU delay require bounded validation.

evidence.description: eventType chooses unbounded event text, redacts before truncation, then emits at most 128 normalized suffix characters; the mapped payload at lines 87-91 contains only exception, message, and request.
The email pattern is /[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}/g, with no preceding token boundary or explicit local-part length bound.
redact invokes detector passes synchronously and has no cancellation, worker isolation, or elapsed-work budget.
The Sentry raw-body limit is one MiB; this is an effective input-byte control but permits a long single type token.
The parser independently enforces the default whole-envelope and event-item byte limits before event mapping; the candidate must remain within both.
Both ingestion controllers use the configured client throttler. A meaningful proof must use a single admitted request, rather than rely on bypassing or exceeding the rate limit.
Plugin events have a 65,536-byte default and 102,400-byte configuration ceiling; the adjacent throttler defaults to 60 requests per 60,000 ms.
The plugin sibling reaches redact through recursive payload cleaning; privacy.ts also applies the same detector set to metadata using hasSensitiveText.
The declared 128-KiB stream message limit is downstream of the Sentry type redaction and can still admit the mapper's small final representation.
The API bootstrap starts one Nest application listener. The reviewed redaction path executes in that application, without a source-visible per-Project worker boundary.

blockers: Complete OS-enforced memory and cumulative-disk sandbox controls are not established, and the assignment forbids all target-controlled execution. No regex fixture, API process, test, or benchmark was run; there is no observed result or retained local artifact.

The supported Bun/JavaScriptCore regex optimizer or fallback behavior may change the cost of this pattern. A safe bounded local check must establish growth within the accepted body sizes and a meaningful delay to unrelated work on the same isolated API process before calling this an availability vulnerability.

validation_plan.local: After the parent establishes all required OS-enforced sandbox controls, use an empty allowlisted environment, no external networking, read-only source/tools, scratch-only writes, low CPU/memory/process/file/disk limits, and a short hard wall-clock deadline. First compare one call to the exact redactor on non-matching ASCII alphabetic strings at small increasing sizes such as 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 bytes, stopping on the first decisive result or deadline. Then, only if the cost warrants it, use an isolated in-memory Sentry controller/service fixture with a dummy verified plugin Credential, fake publisher, header event_id of 32 lowercase hex characters, and an event JSON object containing timestamp: 1, level: info, and type set to the same bounded alphabetic string. Confirm acceptance below the one-MiB caps, observe an independent timer or dummy second-Project request on that same process, and stop at the minimum measurable shared delay. Exercise the plugin sibling separately below its configured byte cap. If the engine remains effectively linear or prevents meaningful shared delay, reject the candidate. Do not send traffic to a deployed API, broker, or provider.

title: Caller timestamps can grow temporal watcher arrays without a bound
description: A plugin Credential holder can submit unique small warning log.line or runtime.restart Events for its bound service while keeping observedAt at one valid timestamp. Each unique Event passes the replay set, and every saved timestamp remains inside inWindow because the comparison uses that same caller timestamp. The error/restart array is then filtered and copied on every input without saturation at the detection threshold. The downstream ten-minute dedupe prevents repeated emitted detections but runs after this work and does not cap sample retention. Source therefore gives linear retained samples and quadratic cumulative array work for a linear number of accepted Events, even when arrival rate respects the API throttle. The shared serial consumer makes this a possible cost imposed on other Projects; no measured delay or availability failure is claimed.
claimed_root_cause: Temporal counting stores every matching timestamp in unbounded arrays and ages them only relative to the next untrusted observedAt. There is no count cap or independent expiration. The 10000-entry replay-ID set bounds only identity storage, and detection dedupe happens after the arrays have already grown and been copied.

trace.description: The producer chooses an ISO timestamp; no freshness, advancement or maximum equal-timestamp sample count is enforced. Project/service binding still applies.
The shared daemon forwards each newly identified warning Event to watcher.ingest with the producer timestamp unchanged.
observe(envelope) evaluates and mutates temporal rule state before createDedupe.accept is called at line 38.
Distinct IDs bypass replay suppression. The bounded observed Set does not limit per-service arrays, and at is parsed directly from observedAt.
All prior samples equal to at satisfy time > at-windowMs and time <= at, regardless of elapsed wall time. Every input scans the full retained array.
The filtered array is copied and appended with no count limit. runtime.restart repeats the same pattern at line 94, retaining growing arrays in the shared watcher's per-service state.

evidence.description: Per-Project/service temporal states have no independent expiry; their errors and restarts arrays survive downstream processing and dedupe.
The restart-count variant filters and spreads all samples even after its threshold of three has been crossed.
The detector only needs small fixed thresholds: five errors or three restarts. No corresponding storage maximum accompanies the configured windows.
Detection dedupe stores a last accepted timestamp and rejects repeated detections, but it cannot undo the preceding temporal-array mutation.
Body and rate limits exist. They do not impose a lifetime sample quota or require producer timestamps to track the arrival clock.
The one consumer awaits each Project's processing serially, making per-Event growing array work part of shared observation dispatch.

blockers: No bounded retained-count or deterministic element-visit observation was performed because complete memory and cumulative disk sandbox controls are unavailable.
Meaningful shared-resource impact has not been measured. Any owner-managed aggregate intake quota or process isolation outside the repository must be inspected before assigning operational impact.

validation_plan.local: In a parent-approved sandbox, call the native createRules/createWatcher interfaces with eight and sixteen unique warning log.line Events containing line=ERROR and one fixed valid observedAt, then repeat the independent runtime.restart variant. Use deterministic inspection of retained counts and array-element visits in a trusted scratch copy, with no more than thirty-two records per variant and no timing-based saturation test. Advance only the fixture's arrival clock to establish whether sample cleanup occurs while observedAt stays fixed. Include a second dummy Project sentinel in the consumer harness. A regression should bound temporal storage and work by the rule threshold/window policy even when equal timestamps persist, while preserving existing threshold behavior.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner can inspect aggregate quotas and daemon/Project process isolation to determine the actual shared blast radius. Do not generate load or send repeated stale-timestamp Events to a deployed service.
